issues.legal_issue: Concurrent factual findings are not reopened on appeal absent an important evidentiary omission or reliance on an irrelevant consideration.
material_facts: The trial court and the High Court found that the disputed lands were joint lands of several estates and rejected the claim that certain estates had been divided.
The Supreme Court found no basis to conclude that the lower courts had overlooked important evidence or relied on an irrelevant consideration.
issues.conclusion: The concurrent findings, including the finding that the estates had not been divided, were not reopened.
issues.legal_principle: The Court stated that it does not ordinarily interfere with concurrent findings of fact unless important evidence was ignored or an irrelevant consideration entered into the decision. No earlier case was cited for this principle.

rule.if: supreme_court_appeal and concurrent_factual_findings and not important_evidence_ignored and not irrelevant_consideration_relied_on

predicates.supreme_court_appeal: The matter is an appeal before the Supreme Court.
predicates.concurrent_factual_findings: The courts below reached the same finding on a factual issue.
predicates.important_evidence_ignored: The lower courts overlooked an important piece of evidence.
predicates.irrelevant_consideration_relied_on: The lower courts relied on an irrelevant consideration in reaching their finding.
predicates.concurrent_finding_left_undisturbed: The concurrent factual finding is left undisturbed.

issues.definition: When a Supreme Court appeal challenges a factual finding shared by the lower courts, the finding remains undisturbed if no important evidence was ignored and no irrelevant consideration was relied on.

issues.legal_issue: The separate-possession revenue rule does not govern a title dispute where the proprietors did not each possess or manage a separate share of the joint estate.
material_facts: The dispute concerned whether land formed part of a joint estate.
The claimant did not assert that each proprietor held or managed a separate share in their own possession or through an agent.
The appellant argued that the lower courts had overlooked section 27 of Regulation VIII of 1793; the Court also found section 23 of that Regulation irrelevant.
issues.conclusion: Section 27 had no bearing on the issues in the case, and section 23 had no relevance to the decision.
issues.legal_principle: Section 27 of Regulation VIII of 1793 addresses revenue settlement where land stands in the joint names of several proprietors but each has a separate share in their own possession and management, or that of an agent. The Court found that circumstance was not asserted here. It also held section 23 irrelevant, noting that it had been repealed in 1805. No earlier case was cited.

predicates.joint_estate_title_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether land belongs to a joint estate.
predicates.no_separate_share_possession_or_manageme: The proprietors are not shown to hold or manage their respective shares separately, personally or through agents.
predicates.separate_possession_revenue_rule_not_app: The separate-possession revenue rule does not govern the dispute.

issues.definition: In a title dispute concerning a joint estate, the separate-possession revenue rule does not apply when the proprietors are not shown to possess or manage separate shares.

issues.legal_issue: A factual contention not raised in the courts below cannot be introduced for the first time in an appeal where its determination requires deciding a question of fact.
material_facts: The appellant argued that the land in its possession did not exceed its share of the joint property.
That contention had not been raised in either the trial court or the High Court.
The Court considered the contention to raise a question of fact.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to consider the contention in the appeal.
issues.legal_principle: A factual plea not raised in the courts below cannot be considered for the first time on appeal when it raises a question of fact. No provision or earlier case was cited for this ruling.

predicates.appeal_from_lower_court_judgment: The proceeding is an appeal from a judgment of lower courts.
predicates.factual_contention_not_raised_below: The party did not raise the factual contention in the courts below.
predicates.contention_requires_fact_finding: Resolving the contention requires deciding a question of fact.
predicates.new_factual_contention_not_considered: The new factual contention is not considered on appeal.

issues.definition: In an appeal from the lower courts, a factual contention is not considered when it was not raised below and its resolution requires a factual determination.

issues.legal_issue: A co-owner’s long exclusive possession does not confer a permanent right against the other co-owners unless the possession is adverse to them.
material_facts: The appellant was found to be a co-owner of the disputed lands.
The appellant relied on long exclusive possession to claim permanent rights.
The appellant had not pleaded adverse possession.
issues.conclusion: The appellant’s long exclusive possession did not confer a permanent right in the lands.
issues.legal_principle: Once a person is found to be a co-owner, possession, however long, does not confer a right against the other co-owners unless it is adverse to them. The Court noted that no plea of adverse possession had been made. No provision or earlier case was cited.

predicates.coownership_established: The person in possession is established to be a co-owner of the property.
predicates.long_exclusive_possession: The co-owner has been in exclusive possession of the property for a long time.
predicates.possession_not_adverse_to_other_coowners: The possession has not been adverse to the other co-owners.
predicates.no_permanent_right_acquired_by_possessio: The possession does not confer a permanent right against the other co-owners.

issues.definition: Long exclusive possession by a co-owner does not confer a permanent right against the other co-owners when that possession is not adverse to them.

issues.legal_issue: A co-owner who receives compensation for acquired jointly owned land must account to another co-owner for that co-owner’s share.
material_facts: The land acquired by the government was found to be part of the joint lands in which the claimant had a share.
The appellant received the compensation for the acquired land.
The acquisition proceedings had proceeded on the basis that the appellant was the owner.
issues.conclusion: The acquisition proceedings did not confer title on the appellant, who was liable to pay the claimant’s share of the compensation.
issues.legal_principle: Acquisition proceedings cannot confer title on a person merely because they proceed on the basis that the person is the owner. Compensation represents the value of the acquired land, and a co-owner who receives it must make over another co-owner’s share. No provision or earlier case was cited.

predicates.claim_for_share_of_acquisition_compensat: The proceeding includes a claim by a co-owner for a share of compensation paid for acquired land.
predicates.coownership_of_acquired_land_established: The claimant is established to be a co-owner of the acquired land.
predicates.compensation_received_by_one_coowner: One co-owner received the compensation for the acquired land.
predicates.recipient_coowner_must_pay_other_coowner: The co-owner who received the compensation must pay the other co-owner’s share.

issues.definition: When a co-owner establishes a claim to compensation for acquired jointly owned land and another co-owner received that compensation, the recipient must pay the claimant’s share.
